title: Parents
hookLine: head east, says the map; the Sigalovada says parents are the east. why that direction?
tomorrow: what could ever repay a parent?

cards: Head east on Main Street, says the map, and nobody asks why east. But back outside Rajagaha, young Sigala is still bowing at dawn to six directions, because his dying father asked him to.

The Buddha keeps the six and gives each one a face. And the first one he names is strange: mother and father are the east. Not the ground under your feet, not the sky above, not the north a compass points to.

teach.b: Here's the honest part first: the Sigalovada doesn't say why. It simply lays out the map. Parents, east.
Teachers, south. Partner and children, west. Friends, north.

teach.h: WHERE THE DAY BEGINS: A READING.
teach.b: Some readers notice that the east is where the sun comes up, where every day begins, the way a life begins with whoever raised it.
That's a reading, not the text, and it's a lovely one, but the sutta leaves the question open. What the text does give is more surprising: the east faces both ways.

A child supports the parents who supported them, helps with their work, keeps the family's ways alive, lives worthy of what they'll inherit, and, after the parents die, makes offerings in their memory.

And parents have five duties of their own: keep their children from harm, encourage them toward good, train them in a skill, help them find a good partner, and hand over the inheritance at the right time.
Done that way, the sutta says, the east is covered, made safe and secure.
So Sigala's bow doesn't change direction. It changes meaning. He's not bowing at empty sky anymore.
He's bowing toward two people, one of whom he has already lost, and toward a promise that runs back and forth between parents and children, long after either side is gone.

how: Some Buddhist families honor parents and ancestors at home shrines and temple festivals, and teachers use the Sigalovada's duties between parents and children when they speak to lay students.

o: ancestors honored only after they've died
mother and father, the east of the six directions
the first two monks to follow the Buddha

games.q: the six directions — tap the pairs.

s: the Sigalovada explains why parents are the east
it doesn't. the sunrise reading is one some readers offer, not the text's own.
in the Sigalovada, parents owe duties to their children too
five of them: keep them from harm, encourage good, train them in a skill, help with a partner, hand over the inheritance.
the Buddha told Sigala to stop bowing to the directions
he kept the six directions and gave each one a face.

games.q: your cousin says the Sigalovada is just a list of what kids owe their parents. you've read it. what's the fair reply?
o: right, it only covers what children must do for parents.
the duties run both ways: five from children, five from parents.
it's mostly about what parents owe kids; children owe very little.
games.why: the east faces both ways: a child supports, helps, keeps the family's ways; a parent guards, encourages, trains, and hands over the inheritance in time.

practice: Find one thing within reach that came from a parent or an elder: a mug, a ring, the way you fold towels. Look at it, or hold it in your mind, and trace it back: who taught you this, and who taught them?
Let the line run east as far as it goes, past names you know to faces you never met.

wordCard.voice: Parents: the east in the Sigalovada, the first direction named. Five duties toward them, and five coming back toward the child.

orig.note: Pali: the eastern direction, which the Sigalovada gives to mother and father.

carryVoice: One word for the day: east, where the day begins and the duties run both ways. Family, one of eleven.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta: the six directions in the noble discipline: parents east, teachers south, wife and children west, friends north, servants and workers below, ascetics and brahmins above; the five duties of children to parents and of parents to children; 'thus the east is covered, made safe and secure')
